title: Awakening, Mumonkan 19 and the Best Things I've Found
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up awakening through Mumonkan case 19, in which Nansen tells Joshu that ordinary mind is the way. Seishu gathers views from Susan Moon, Dale Wright, Joan Sutherland, Suzuki Roshi, and Norman Fischer's book What Is Zen?, then looks for enlightened activity in daily life. The examples are Norman handing his cup of tea to a coughing woman at a Bellingham retreat, the patient nurses who cared for Seishu's wife after knee surgery, and a friendly checker in a crowded Fred Meyer. Seishu closes with a passage on nirvana from Karen Armstrong's Buddha and the story of Seishu's father, who died in 2002 at 90, frail and cheerful, telling Seishu, "It's okay to die if you've had a good life."

sentences.text: If you are a practitioner with Red Cedar, you do know John, and I'm grateful to him because he definitely was one of my mentors.
So thank you very much, John.
He's been practicing Zen since 1995 and received lay entrustment through Zoketsu Norman Fischer in 2010.
So thank you for coming online to give a talk to us, John.
And thank you very much.
Thank you, Chris.
I guess we'll start with our chant for entering or starting the Dharma talk.
Okay.
*Unsurpassed, penetrating and perfect Dharma is rarely met with, even in 100,000 million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Well, good morning and welcome everyone.
And Chris, now you've become my mentor, so it's nice how things go around.
I so appreciate all the things you do for Red Cedar and all the energy and effort you put out for us.
Thank you very much.
As many of you know, this topic of awakening or enlightenment has been the subject of our talks the last several weeks, and I'll continue that.
It's been an interesting topic to read about and research.
I've always appreciated the many Zen stories of encounters between teachers and students that we've inherited from ancient China and Japan.
Even though I often have a hard time understanding the meaning, the dialogues usually end with an awakening experience.
One of my favorites is one that many of you are familiar with.
It's case 19 from the Mumonkan, "Ordinary mind is the way."
I'm just going to read you the case.
*Joshu asked Nansen, "What is the way?"
Nansen said, "Ordinary mind is the way."
Joshu asked, "Should I try to direct myself toward it?"
And Nansen said, "If you try to direct yourself, you betray your own practice."
Joshu asked, "How can I know the way if I don't direct myself?"
And Nansen said, "The way is not subject to knowing or not knowing.
Knowing is delusion, not knowing is blankness.
If you truly reach the way, you will find it as vast and boundless as outer space.
How can this be discussed at the level of affirmation or negation?"*
*And with these words, Joshu had sudden realization.*
Buddhism needs awakening.
I'm pretty sure that if the Buddha hadn't had his great enlightenment experience, we wouldn't be sitting here today.

And I'm also pretty sure that one of the reasons Buddhism has existed for over 2,500 years, and has been passed on from person to person for all of these years, is in part because awakened teachers were inspired to pass on the practice, and students were inspired by the teachings and also by the qualities of the teachers.
I know for myself, I have certainly been inspired by both: by the teachings and by the qualities of the various teachers I've worked with over the years.
But even so, when I started practice, it wasn't because I was seeking enlightenment or was even interested in it.
I was doing well in my life at the time.

But I was afraid that I would not be able to handle the big challenges that I knew were sure to happen sooner or later: death of parents, loved ones, friends, illness, my own aging and death, things like that.
I was doing well just because my life was going well, but I had no tools for dealing with hardship, and it scared me.
Once I started practice, I figured that enlightenment was for men and women who lived in monasteries for many years.
I didn't think that it would be possible for someone like me who had a family and a job and only practiced part time.

In the beginning of practice, I was mostly concerned with finding a meditation posture that I could maintain without too much pain, and then how to handle pain, physical pain and emotional pain, when it came up.
And then of course learning to pay attention to posture and breathing.
You're also learning to observe thoughts and feelings and memories and all of the things that come up in the mind, and all the things the senses pick up while you're meditating.
And then of course when I get caught by those things, I come back to posture and breath.
So, training the mind.
I was learning to pay more attention to my words and to my actions, and to the results of those choices that I made, and then to notice mistakes and try to make corrections when I noticed them.
It was also really helpful to learn about and pay more attention to Buddhist concepts like impermanence, that everything is moving and changing, that nothing lasts.
And to notice how suffering is created, how so much suffering can be created by how we react to things.

And also, unbeknownst to me, I wasn't even looking for this, I discovered the blessing of practicing with other people: sitting together, working together, studying together, and supporting each other through life's joys and struggles.
That's been a tremendous gift.
I'm not ever pushing for enlightenment, but I've been really satisfied with the way that practice over the years has impacted my life.

So, coming back to the topic of enlightenment, I thought I would just share some of the best things that I came across in doing research for this talk, some of the things I read, some of the Dharma talks that I listened to.
One of the things I listened to was a panel discussion by senior students from the Everyday Zen Foundation on the topic of enlightenment.
The Everyday Zen Foundation was started by our founding teacher Norman Fischer down in the Bay Area.
One of the participants in this panel discussion is Susan Moon.
She talked about preferring the term awakening, because that's a verb.
It's something that can happen over and over again.
It's not a noun, like enlightenment, and it's also not something that you either have or you don't have.

In a similar vein, Dale Wright, who is a Buddhist practitioner, scholar and writer, mentioned in one of his books that, like everything in Buddhism, enlightenment, if it arises, is dependent on factors outside of itself.
It's impermanent, and it changes along with everything else.
Another source of information for me was the book *What Is Zen?* by Norman Fischer and Susan Moon.
In this book Susan asks Norman many, many questions about Zen practice, and there's a whole section on enlightenment.
She asked Norman, will regular Zen practice lead to an enlightening experience or a breakthrough?
And Norman answers:
*There isn't a one size fits all experience.
You might have a big one if you practice in a tradition that emphasizes that, and our style, Soto Zen, does not.
But there are many kinds of experiences that happen over the years that are transformative.
It's possible to look back over many years of practice and see big changes without being able to pinpoint exactly where or when those changes occurred.*
And Suzuki Roshi, the priest who came from Japan in the 1950s and founded the San Francisco Zen Center, used to compare practicing Soto Zen to walking in a mist.
It doesn't seem like you're getting wet, but eventually your robes are soaked.
So Soto Zen is a long, gradual, gentle practice.
Norman emphasized the importance of regular ongoing practice so that any awakening experience can be settled and embodied and brought into day to day life.
And this is only possible with an ongoing practice.
Then one other takeaway from that section of the book: Norman defined an enlightened person as someone with wisdom and a good heart.
And then he listed the qualities mentioned in the six Buddhist paramitas, or perfections, which are generosity, patience, ethical conduct, effort, meditation, and wisdom.

And the 13th century Japanese priest who is considered the founder of Soto Zen mentions four activities of enlightened people: giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and identity action, which he defines as acting with the interests of others in mind.
So an enlightened person acts for the benefit of others.

And then the last thing in his talk on enlightenment: Norman said that the main goal of Buddhism is the development of a good heart with compassion and insight into the nature of reality of our lives, seeing our inner connection with all things.
I would also like to read you a couple paragraphs from an article entitled "What Is Enlightenment?" by Joan Sutherland.
Joan's a teacher in the Zen koan tradition who lives in Santa Fe, New Mexico, and I'm pretty sure their tradition does emphasize trying for the big enlightenment experience.
But here are a couple things that she had to say.
*Awakening is more like a path than an event.
It has steps and aspects, leaps forward and stumbles.
What we awaken to is the same for all of us.
How we awaken and express that awakening in our lives is endlessly idiosyncratic and gives the world its texture and delight.*
And then later in that article she says:
*It's more like we've been living in two dimensions, and now there are three.
Strawberries still taste like strawberries, and harsh words are still harsh words.
But now we are aware of how everything penetrates everything else, and that even the most difficult things are lit from within by the same undivided light.*
And the last comment from her:
*We have bodies that break down in all sorts of amazing ways.
We still face injustice and conflict.
Awakening isn't a waiver from the shared circumstances of human life, but it does radically transform how we experience them.

We are no longer beleaguered exiles but now people at home, even in the most difficult times, searching for ways to respond that encourage the bursting forth of enlightenment that is present always and everywhere.*
And then one last sentence from Suzuki Roshi:
*There is no such thing as an enlightened person.
There is only enlightened activity.*

After all this reading and research, one thing I thought I'd do a few weeks ago is just keep an eye out in my day to day life and see if I could see any enlightened activity, either something that I just encountered, or maybe something I remembered from the past.
One of the first things I thought of was an event that happened at a meditation retreat several years ago in Bellingham.
It was with our founding teacher Norman Fischer, who was up from the Bay Area.
We were in the Dharma hall and I think it was a Saturday morning.
He was just getting ready to give a Dharma talk.
So we had done the chant that we just did here this morning.
Incense was lit, and someone had placed a teacup in front of him, and he was just starting his talk when a woman sitting right near him began to cough.
And Norman immediately, just as smooth as could be, reached over, put out the incense, grabbed his cup of tea and handed it to the woman, and she took a couple sips and she stopped coughing.

It was just a little simple thing, but it was as automatic and smooth as you could imagine, and it seemed like the best possible response to that situation, which to me seems like a good definition of enlightened activity.
Again it was just a little event, but it really registered with me, so I wanted to mention that.
And then another example, or a number of examples: at the end of March, my wife had knee replacement surgery at St.
Joe's Hospital and she was there for a day and a half, and I spent time in her room just sitting with her and visiting and stuff like that.
And I was so impressed with
the care she got from the nurses.
Every time a nurse came into the room they were kind and patient.
They're so busy, they have so many people to take care of, it's a very demanding job, but there wasn't ever a hint of stress or pressure or upset.
Carolyn would ask, "Could I need this or this, and could I have that?" and they were, "Oh yes dear, I'll get that for you."
It was just a really moving and powerful thing to see.
I was very happy that she was being so well cared for.
It set a very high standard for me once we got home and it became my job to do those things.
The last example I thought of is again just a little trivial thing from day to day life, but I was at Fred Meyer.
A couple weeks ago, on a really busy evening, the store was quite crowded, all the automatic checkout things were full, and there were long lines at every in-person counter.
Some people had big full baskets and some people looked pretty impatient.
They weren't happy about having to wait in line.
So I thought, boy, when I get to the front of the line I bet the checker's going to be either stressed or something.
But this checker was extremely friendly: "How's your day going?
I hope you're having a good day."
We had a little chat and she was very friendly.
It was quite unexpected and kind of uplifting.
Maybe it's a little bit of a stretch to call that enlightened activity, but it really kind of boosted me a little bit.

I don't know about you, but in this pandemic I don't have very many face to face conversations with people other than my wife, so these little encounters I think have a lot more impact these days, and I really appreciated that.
So I wanted to mention it.
I also thought, even though my talk will soon be over, I'm going to keep an eye out for enlightened activity in my day to day life.
I'm really kind of enjoying watching that, and it's uplifting to see it, and it actually happens more often than you might think.
To finish my talk, I'm going to read a page from a book by Karen Armstrong, and then I'm going to tell you a personal story about my father.
This book is called *Buddha*.
It's a biography of the Buddha with quite a bit of information about Buddhist practice, the four noble truths, eightfold path, that kind of thing.
Karen Armstrong was a Catholic nun for 12 years and then became a religious writer.
She's written about all the major religions, and she's really an excellent writer.
I highly recommend this book.
This page is about Nirvana, and here's what she says.
*The attainment of Nirvana did not mean that the Buddha would never experience any more suffering.
He would grow old, get sick and die like everybody else, and experience pain while doing so.

Nirvana does not give a person trance-like immunity, but an inner haven, which enables a man or a woman to live with pain, to take possession of it, affirm it and experience a profound peace of mind in the midst of suffering.
Nirvana, therefore, is found within oneself, in the very heart of each person's being.
It's an entirely natural state; it is not bestowed by grace, nor achieved for us by a supernatural Savior.
It can be reached by anybody who cultivates the path as assiduously as the Buddha did.
Nirvana is a still center; it gives meaning to life.*
*Once a person has learned to access this nucleus of calm, he or she is no longer driven by conflicting fears and desires, and is able to face pain, sorrow and grief with equanimity.
An enlightened or awakened human being has discovered a strength within that comes from being correctly centered, beyond the reach of selfishness.*
So this passage reminds me of how my father faced his death.
He died in 2002 at the age of 90.
He was born in New York City and grew up in New York till he was 12 or 13, attending Catholic schools.
But he had some bad experiences there with the priests and nuns, who were really harsh.
A lot of hitting with sticks and things like that.
So as an adult, he had no interest in practicing religion.
He was always a very athletic, very active guy, and he played football and boxed in college.
And then as an adult he was always doing lots of sports, so as a family we did lots of sports.
We skied and hiked and played tennis and things like that, and he stayed active his whole life.
In the 1980s, he got dementia and congestive heart failure, so over a few years he became very frail.
By the end of his life he was just a shell of himself really.
He was very frail, very feeble.
He was wearing diapers.
He couldn't feed himself in the last few weeks, and it was very difficult to talk.
But what was amazing to me is that he stayed cheerful.
He smiled a lot.
He was happy to see people.
He would joke occasionally, and he almost never complained.
I remember thinking as I spent time with him, how can he do that?
How could he be content and cheerful in the condition he's in?
He's lost everything.
One of the last things he said to me was, "It's okay to die if you've had a good life."
So he knew that he was dying and he accepted it, and he was peaceful about it.
The other thing I remember thinking was, when my time comes I want to be like him.
I want to be content with my life.
I want to be cheerful, I want to be happy to see people.
And he handled all that so well.
I remember feeling inspired by that, and I still feel inspired by it.
I can't imagine handling your death any better than that.
So I thought that would be a good story to tell, and I wanted to share that with you.
I think that's about all I have to say on the subject of awakening and enlightenment, so I want to thank you for listening.
We'll do our little chant to end the talk, and then I think there's time for discussion or questions if anybody has any comments.
So, let's do our chant.
Thank you for listening.
*May our intentions equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.*
